questions.stem: Top-level managers, such as a chief executive officer, are mainly responsible for:
options: setting the long-term objectives and strategy of the business
supervising the daily tasks of employees on the shop floor
processing customer orders and handling routine enquiries
carrying out the weekly plans set for their own department
questions.explanation: Top managers make strategic decisions about the direction of the whole business over several years. Supervising daily work is the role of first-line managers.

questions.stem: First-line managers are best described as managers who:
options: report only to the shareholders at the annual meeting
directly supervise employees doing the day-to-day work
set the overall direction of the business for the board
coordinate several departments across different states
questions.explanation: First-line managers, such as supervisors and team leaders, oversee the daily work of operational staff and report to middle managers. Setting overall direction is the role of top managers.

questions.stem: A regional manager for a supermarket chain turns the head office's annual sales targets into plans for the 12 stores in her area. She is acting as a:
options: first-line manager
board director
middle manager
top-level manager
questions.explanation: Middle managers translate top managers' strategies into plans for their division or region and coordinate the first-line managers below them.

questions.stem: At a Newcastle manufacturing company, which decision is most likely to be made by a first-line manager rather than by top or middle management?
options: setting the annual production budget for the whole manufacturing division
choosing which overseas markets the company should enter over five years
allocating this week's shifts to the workers on one production line
deciding whether the company should build a new factory in Queensland
questions.explanation: First-line managers make short-term, operational decisions about their own team. A new factory and overseas markets are strategic top-level decisions, and divisional budgets are usually set by middle managers.

questions.stem: The management function of planning involves:
options: setting goals and deciding how they will be achieved
comparing actual results with targets after the event
motivating and communicating with employees each day
arranging staff and resources into departments and teams
questions.explanation: Planning sets objectives and the strategies to reach them. Comparing results with targets is controlling, motivating is leading and arranging resources is organising.

questions.stem: The manager of a Gosford cafe draws up a roster, assigns each staff member a role and orders the equipment needed for a new menu. Which management function is she mainly performing?
options: organising
planning
leading
controlling
questions.explanation: Organising arranges people, tasks and resources so that plans can be carried out. Deciding on the new menu would be planning; the roster and equipment put that plan into effect.

questions.stem: A manager holds regular team meetings, praises good work and explains why changes are being made. Which management function is this?
options: planning
leading
organising
controlling
questions.explanation: Leading involves motivating, communicating with and guiding employees towards goals. Organising concerns structure and resources, not inspiring people.

questions.stem: A Dubbo retailer finds that monthly sales are 12 per cent below target and launches a promotion to close the gap. Which management function does this show?
options: controlling
organising
leading
planning
questions.explanation: Controlling means measuring actual performance, comparing it with planned targets and taking corrective action. The target came from planning, but checking against it and responding is controlling.

questions.stem: Why are the four functions of management described as a continuous cycle?
options: results found in controlling are used to revise future plans
each function is performed only once when a business starts
managers must complete organising before any planning occurs
controlling replaces planning once a business is established
questions.explanation: Controlling compares results with plans, and what managers learn feeds back into new or revised plans, so the functions repeat continuously. Planning normally comes before organising, not after.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of leadership improving employee engagement?
options: a manager installs cameras to check that staff are working at every moment of the day
a manager cuts the training budget so staff can spend more time on tasks
a manager tells staff that their ideas will not be needed in future
a manager involves staff in setting team goals and recognises their progress
questions.explanation: Engaged employees are committed and willing to give extra effort; leaders build this through involvement, recognition and clear purpose. Close surveillance and ignoring ideas tend to reduce engagement.

questions.stem: How does leadership most influence corporate culture?
options: leaders set the culture once and it never changes afterwards
leaders' behaviour models the values and norms that staff adopt
leaders can change the culture instantly by issuing a new policy
leadership has no effect, because culture is set only by law
questions.explanation: Culture is the shared values and ways of doing things in a business, and staff take their cues from what leaders actually do. A written policy alone rarely changes culture quickly.

questions.stem: A Sydney insurer is moving all its claims processing to a new digital system. Which leadership action is most likely to build change readiness among staff?
options: announcing the change on the day the new system goes live
keeping the plans secret so that staff do not become worried about them
warning staff that anyone who struggles will lose their job
explaining the reasons for the change and offering training early
questions.explanation: Change readiness grows when staff understand why change is needed and feel able to cope with it, so communication and training reduce resistance. Secrecy and threats increase fear and resistance.

questions.stem: Two team leaders at a Penrith warehouse are in conflict over shared forklifts, and orders are being delayed. Which leadership response is most likely to resolve the conflict in the long term?
options: meeting both leaders, identifying the cause and agreeing on a fair allocation
ignoring the dispute in the hope that the two leaders will sort it out alone
taking all the forklifts away from both teams until the dispute ends
blaming the leader who complains most often and ending the matter there
questions.explanation: Effective conflict resolution addresses the underlying cause, here access to a shared resource, and reaches an agreed solution. Ignoring the conflict or punishing one side leaves the cause in place.

questions.stem: An autocratic leadership style is one in which the manager:
options: makes decisions alone and expects employees to follow instructions
shares decision-making with employees and seeks their agreement
leaves employees to make most decisions without any involvement
makes decisions only after a majority vote of the company's shareholders
questions.explanation: Autocratic leaders keep authority and decision-making to themselves and use clear directions. Sharing decisions with staff describes a democratic style.

questions.stem: A democratic leadership style involves the manager:
options: avoiding any communication with employees about decisions
involving employees in decisions and valuing their input
making every decision alone and closely supervising staff
giving employees instructions without explaining the reasons
questions.explanation: Democratic leaders consult and involve employees, which can improve commitment and the quality of ideas. Making decisions alone with close supervision is autocratic.

questions.stem: A gas leak is detected at a Port Botany factory and staff must leave the site immediately. Which leadership style suits this situation?
options: autocratic, because staff can never be trusted to make decisions
autocratic, because quick, clear instructions are needed
democratic, because staff should vote on how to evacuate
democratic, because staff are more committed to shared decisions
questions.explanation: In an emergency there is no time for consultation, so direct instructions keep people safe. Autocratic leadership suits the situation, not a belief that staff are untrustworthy.

questions.stem: A team of experienced designers at a Surry Hills agency is creating a new brand campaign with no tight deadline. Which leadership style is most suitable?
options: autocratic, because creative work needs close supervision
autocratic, because designers dislike being asked for ideas
democratic, because the manager has no authority over them
democratic, because skilled staff can contribute valuable ideas
questions.explanation: Skilled, motivated employees doing creative work with time available benefit from a democratic style that draws on their expertise. Close supervision would waste their skills and may lower engagement.

questions.stem: A manager uses a democratic style for every decision, including urgent ones. Which problem is most likely?
options: employees feel excluded from all decision-making
staff have too little say in how their work is done
the manager loses all legal authority over the staff
decisions are delayed when quick action is needed
questions.explanation: Consultation takes time, so relying on it for urgent decisions slows the business down. Leaders should match their style to the situation, using an autocratic approach when speed matters.

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly calls for an autocratic rather than a democratic style?
options: deciding with long-serving staff how to arrange a new office
training new casual staff to follow strict food safety procedures
planning a staff social event with an experienced, motivated team
seeking ideas from senior engineers to improve a product design
questions.explanation: Inexperienced staff learning procedures that must be followed exactly need clear direction. The other situations involve experienced staff and decisions where their input adds value, which suits a democratic style.

questions.stem: Which list shows the stages of the business life cycle in order?
options: establishment, growth, maturity, then decline or renewal
growth, establishment, maturity, then decline or renewal
establishment, maturity, growth, then decline or renewal
maturity, establishment, growth, then decline or renewal
questions.explanation: A business is established, grows as sales rise, reaches maturity as growth levels off, and then either declines or renews itself through new products, markets or strategies.

questions.stem: A Coffs Harbour tour company opened eight months ago. Sales are low, the owner works long hours and cash is tight as she builds a customer base. Which stage is it in?
options: growth
maturity
decline
establishment
questions.explanation: The establishment stage features low sales, building awareness and a customer base, and cash flow pressure as start-up costs are paid. Growth begins when sales rise rapidly.

questions.stem: A Sydney meal-kit business's sales have levelled off, competitors have copied its products and most potential customers already know the brand. Which stage is it in?
options: renewal
maturity
growth
establishment
questions.explanation: In maturity, sales growth slows or stops because the market is saturated and competition is strong. Renewal would involve new products or markets to restart growth.

questions.stem: Which challenge is most typical of the establishment stage?
options: keeping long-serving staff motivated in a large firm
renewing products that customers have grown tired of
coordinating many departments across several states
managing cash flow while sales are still low
questions.explanation: New businesses face high start-up costs and low, uncertain sales, so cash flow is a key challenge. Large, long-established businesses face the other problems.

questions.stem: A Wollongong bakery has grown from one shop to six in two years. Which challenge is it most likely to face at this stage?
options: closing the business as demand for its products disappears
finding ways to renew sales after years of no growth at all
delegating to new managers and maintaining quality across sites
attracting its very first customers and building brand awareness
questions.explanation: In the growth stage the owner can no longer oversee everything, so recruiting and delegating to managers, formalising systems and keeping quality consistent become key challenges. Finding first customers belongs to establishment.

questions.stem: A long-established Orange cider maker has had flat sales for five years. Its managers resist new ideas because 'what we do has always worked'. Which risk does this maturity-stage challenge create?
options: a lack of brand awareness may stop customers trying it
complacency may lead to decline as competitors innovate
rapid growth may outstrip the firm's production capacity
start-up costs may cause a cash shortage in its first year
questions.explanation: Mature businesses can become complacent and resistant to change, letting more innovative rivals take market share and pushing the business towards decline. Capacity limits are a growth-stage challenge.

questions.stem: Research and development (R&D) in a business involves:
options: surveying customers to find how satisfied they are with service
recording and analysing the business's financial transactions
recruiting and training staff to fill new positions in the business
investigating and creating new or improved products and processes
questions.explanation: R&D investigates new knowledge and turns it into new or improved products, services and processes. Customer satisfaction surveys are market research.

questions.stem: A mature appliance maker with falling sales invests in R&D to develop a new energy-efficient range. This is most likely aimed at:
options: liquidation, by selling assets to pay its creditors
decline, by allowing sales to fall away gradually
renewal, by giving customers a new reason to buy
establishment, by building its first customer base
questions.explanation: R&D can renew a mature or declining business by creating new products that restart growth. Without renewal, a mature business is likely to decline.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates spending heavily on R&D?
options: it is useful only in the establishment stage and wasted after that
it lowers costs immediately, so profit rises in the same year
it can drive growth and renewal but is costly and its results are uncertain
it guarantees successful new products, so it carries no financial risk
questions.explanation: R&D can create a competitive advantage and new sources of revenue, but it takes time and money and many projects fail. Businesses must weigh the potential long-term benefits against the cost and risk.

questions.stem: A profitable Bathurst builder fails because customers pay months late while its suppliers and staff must be paid on time. Which reason for failure does this show?
options: a change in consumer tastes
poor cash flow management
a lack of customer demand
excessive investment in R&D
questions.explanation: A business can be profitable on paper yet run out of cash if inflows arrive later than outflows. Demand was strong here; the problem was the timing of cash.

questions.stem: Which is an external reason for business decline?
options: staff receive no training and make frequent mistakes
a new technology makes the business's main product obsolete
the owner keeps poor records and does not monitor the business's expenses
managers fail to plan for growth and run out of stock
questions.explanation: External factors, such as technological change, recessions, new competitors and changing tastes, come from outside the business. Poor records, planning and training are internal management weaknesses.

questions.stem: A Wagga Wagga video-rental store closed as customers switched to streaming, although its owner had cut costs and kept good records. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: businesses fail only because of poor decisions made by their owners
external change can cause failure even when internal management is sound
the store failed mainly because the owner kept poor financial records
the store would have survived if it had simply raised its prices
questions.explanation: A shift in technology and consumer behaviour destroyed demand regardless of how efficiently the store was run. Good management helps, but businesses must also adapt to external change to survive.

questions.stem: Business acquisition as a voluntary exit strategy means that:
options: a court orders the business to be closed and its assets sold
the owner is declared bankrupt by the court at a creditor's request
an administrator takes control of the business from its directors
the owner sells the business to another business or buyer
questions.explanation: In an acquisition, another business or buyer purchases the business, and the owner exits by choice and receives payment. Court orders and administrators are involuntary processes.

questions.stem: The owner of a solvent Armidale newsagency decides to retire. No buyer is found, so she sells the stock, pays all debts and closes the shop. This is:
options: involuntary liquidation
voluntary administration
a business acquisition
voluntary business closure
questions.explanation: Voluntary closure is a planned decision by the owner to stop trading while the business can still pay its debts. Liquidation and administration are insolvency processes, and no buyer means no acquisition.

questions.stem: Why might the owner of a successful cafe prefer acquisition to voluntary closure when exiting?
options: acquisition lets the owner keep receiving all future profits
a buyer may pay for goodwill as well as the physical assets
acquisition removes the need to pay any of the cafe's debts
closure is not allowed by law for a business that is solvent
questions.explanation: A going concern can be sold for more than its stock and equipment because the buyer also gains its customers, reputation and location (goodwill). Debts must still be settled, and the new owner receives future profits.

questions.stem: A business is insolvent when it:
options: cannot pay its debts as and when they fall due
makes a loss in a single financial year
has more current assets than current liabilities
decides to stop trading and close voluntarily
questions.explanation: ASIC describes an insolvent company as one that cannot pay its debts when they are due. A single loss does not make a business insolvent if it can still meet its debts.

questions.stem: A sole trader in Tamworth cannot pay debts of $180,000 and her creditors take action. Which process applies to her as an individual?
options: bankruptcy
liquidation
voluntary administration
a deed of company arrangement
questions.explanation: Bankruptcy is an insolvency procedure for individuals, including sole traders with unlimited liability; it does not apply to companies. Liquidation, voluntary administration and deeds of company arrangement are company procedures.

questions.stem: In voluntary administration, the directors of an insolvent company:
options: keep full control while creditors decide how much they will be repaid
are declared bankrupt and must sell their own homes to pay creditors
must immediately sell all the company's assets and close the business
appoint an independent administrator who takes control to try to save it
questions.explanation: Directors who believe the company is or may become insolvent can appoint an independent registered liquidator as voluntary administrator, who takes control and works out whether the company or its business can be saved. Directors lose control during the administration.

questions.stem: At the end of a voluntary administration, creditors vote on the company's future. Which is one of the outcomes they can choose?
options: extend the administration indefinitely so that no debts are ever paid
accept a deed of company arrangement setting out how debts will be dealt with
declare the company bankrupt so that its directors repay all debts personally
transfer ownership of the company to the largest creditor at no cost
questions.explanation: Creditors can return the company to the directors, accept a deed of company arrangement, or put the company into liquidation. Companies cannot be made bankrupt, since bankruptcy applies only to individuals.

questions.stem: When a company goes into liquidation:
options: the directors keep running it as normal while they look for new investors
its shareholders become personally liable for all of its debts
the government takes ownership and keeps the business trading
a liquidator sells its assets and distributes the proceeds to creditors
questions.explanation: In liquidation an independent liquidator winds up the company's affairs, selling assets and paying creditors in order, after which the company is deregistered. Shareholders of a limited company are not personally liable for its debts.

questions.stem: A company that is still solvent wants to close because its owners are retiring. Which form of liquidation applies?
options: a court liquidation
a voluntary administration
a members' voluntary liquidation
a creditors' voluntary liquidation
questions.explanation: ASIC describes a members' voluntary liquidation as one for solvent companies, initiated by shareholders. A creditors' voluntary liquidation is for insolvent companies, and voluntary administration is not a form of liquidation.
